newsitem.title: USA: Critics say agency conceals wild horse slaughter.
newsitem.headline: Critics say agency conceals wild horse slaughter.

text.p: Government workers and animal activists accused a federal agency Monday of covering up the slaughter of wild horses from public rangelands in the West.

Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility said Bureau of Land Management agents "claim the agency has tolerated and in some cases facilitated the routine and illegal trafficking of wild horses to slaughter."

PEER and the American Wild Horse and Burro Alliance told a news conference the Interior Department's Bureau of Land Management had reduced wild horse and burro populations to 18,000-20,000 and said half the herds were too small to be sustainable.

"The American people need to know that wild horses and burros are being systematically eradicated and used as a scapegoat for causing the destruction of our public lands," the alliance said in a statement.

But the agency said its counts show there are 42,000 wild horses and burros and all the herds are at sustainable levels. It also said its checks showed 350 wild horses were being sent to slaughter annually, not the thousands that critics contend.
"We continue to say if there is any evidence more are going to slaughter give us the evidence," agency spokesman Bob Johns said.
But Jim Baca, BLM director from 1993 to February 1994, said the Clinton administration should have a special administrator assess the wild horse and burro programme.

Representative Steven Schiff, a New Mexico Republican, plans to call for a congressional hearing or an investigation by the General Accounting Office, Congress' watchdog agency, into the wild horse programme, Schiff's spokesman said.

Animal advocates say thousands of horses that were supposed to get federal protection were slaughtered after they were bought through an adoption programme. They also say horses were stolen, misbranded and moved through difficult-to-trace areas on their way to slaughter or other commercial use.

The Humane Society of the United States and other groups said the BLM did not adequately screen buyers or monitor horses before titles were passed on for adoption. They also said the $125 per horse adoption fee was too low.
The bureau has argued there was no reason for anyone adopting an animal to sell a horse to slaughter for $500 when it cost $1,000 to maintain one for the year until the adoption became official.
